articles.title: Exclusive: Armenia Eyes India’s New 120 km Guided Pinaka Rocket, Could Become Launch Customer
articles.text:
Armenia could emerge as the first international customer for India’s upcoming 120 km Guided Pinaka rocket, building upon its existing investment in the 75 km Guided Pinaka system. idrw.org has learned from its sources that the extended-range guided rocket is progressing through developmental trials and is expected to receive production clearance by mid-2027, after which it will be actively marketed to friendly foreign countries.
According to sources familiar with the programme, Armenia has been kept informed of the missile’s development progress because it already operates the Guided Pinaka system, making the transition to the longer-range rocket both operationally and logistically straightforward.
The 120 km Guided Pinaka is being developed as the next evolution of India’s indigenous multi-barrel rocket launcher (MBRL) family. While retaining compatibility with existing Pinaka launchers, the new rocket significantly extends engagement range, allowing artillery units to strike high-value targets much deeper inside enemy territory without requiring entirely new launcher platforms or support infrastructure.
For existing Pinaka users, this commonality offers a major advantage. The same launch vehicles, command-and-control systems, logistics chain and maintenance infrastructure can be utilised while substantially increasing operational reach. Such compatibility reduces lifecycle costs and simplifies future upgrades for overseas customers.
idrw.org sources indicate that once production begins, India intends to offer the 120 km Guided Pinaka to several friendly nations as part of its expanding defence export strategy. Armenia, having become the first foreign customer for the Guided Pinaka family, is expected to receive one of the earliest offers for the upgraded rocket.
For Armenia, the enhanced range would strengthen its long-range precision artillery capability without introducing an entirely new weapon system into service. Instead, the country could expand the capabilities of its existing Pinaka inventory through the acquisition of compatible extended-range ammunition.
The longer-range rocket also has broader export potential.
Many countries are seeking cost-effective alternatives to expensive tactical ballistic missiles for engaging command posts, logistics hubs, artillery concentrations and other military targets beyond the reach of conventional tube artillery. Guided rocket artillery has gained increasing prominence following recent conflicts, where precision long-range fires have played a decisive role in battlefield operations.
The Pinaka system has already demonstrated India’s growing ability to compete in the international rocket artillery market. An extended-range 120 km variant would further enhance its competitiveness against comparable systems offered by established global manufacturers.
India’s defence industry has increasingly focused on developing scalable weapon families that allow customers to upgrade capabilities without replacing entire platforms. The Guided Pinaka roadmap reflects this philosophy, enabling operators to progressively extend range and precision while retaining common logistics and support infrastructure.
The expected induction of the 120 km Guided Pinaka into Indian service will also strengthen its export prospects. International customers often prefer systems that have already entered operational service with the manufacturing country’s armed forces, providing greater confidence in long-term support and production sustainability.
According to idrw.org sources, developmental trials are progressing as planned, with production approval anticipated around mid-2027. Once manufacturing begins, the extended-range rocket is expected to become a key component of India’s expanding defence export portfolio alongside systems such as the BrahMos missile, Akash air defence system and other indigenous precision-guided weapons.
If Armenia proceeds with a follow-on acquisition, it would further deepen defence cooperation between New Delhi and Yerevan while reinforcing India’s position as an increasingly important supplier of advanced artillery and precision-strike systems to international partners.

articles.title: LCA Mk2 PV1 Is Moving Ahead: ADA Seeks New Automated System to Test Fighter’s Cable Harnesses
articles.text:
The Aeronautical Development Agency (ADA) has issued a specialised tender for automatic cable harness testing of the LCA Air Force Mk2 Prototype Vehicle 1 (PV1), providing another indication that India’s indigenous medium-weight fighter programme is progressing into detailed aircraft integration and systems-validation activities.
The tender, identified as GEM/2026/B/7909097, was published by ADA on August 12, 2026, with bids scheduled to close on August 22. The approximately five-month work package is specifically linked to PV1, making it particularly relevant to the first prototype’s ongoing assembly and integration programme.
The requirement involves automated testing of the extensive electrical and avionics wiring harnesses installed throughout the aircraft. Such harnesses form the nervous system of a modern combat aircraft, connecting flight-control computers, sensors, avionics line-replaceable units, power systems, communications equipment and other mission-critical systems.
For an aircraft as complex as the LCA Mk2, manually checking thousands of electrical connections would be extremely time-consuming and would make it more difficult to identify intermittent faults or wiring errors. Automated harness-testing equipment can systematically verify continuity, insulation, connectivity and electrical characteristics while helping engineers identify incorrect connections and potential faults before the aircraft’s systems are powered up.
The timing of the tender is particularly significant because PV1 is the first flying prototype of the LCA Mk2 programme. As the aircraft progresses from structural assembly toward systems integration, validating the electrical architecture becomes an essential prerequisite for subsequent power-on and ground-testing activities.
The LCA Mk2 is considerably larger and more sophisticated than the Tejas Mk1/Mk1A. It is designed as a medium-weight multirole fighter with increased internal fuel, greater payload capacity and a substantially expanded avionics architecture. The aircraft is also planned to use the General Electric F414 engine, providing a higher thrust class than the F404 powering the existing Tejas variants.
The harness-testing requirement therefore provides a glimpse into an otherwise largely invisible part of aircraft development. While radar, engines and weapons tend to dominate attention, the reliability of the electrical architecture can determine whether those systems can actually operate together as an integrated combat aircraft.
For the first prototype, this is particularly important. Electrical faults discovered after an aircraft has entered advanced systems testing can result in significant delays because engineers may have to access wiring buried deep inside the airframe. Detecting such problems before power-on can reduce troubleshooting time and minimise disruption to the integration schedule.
The five-month duration of the contract also suggests that the activity is expected to cover a substantial portion of the prototype’s wiring architecture rather than being a simple one-time inspection.
The tender comes as the LCA Mk2 programme approaches a series of important milestones. HAL is progressing with prototype manufacturing and assembly, while ADA continues to place contracts for individual systems and specialised integration activities required for the aircraft.
The broader significance is that PV1 is increasingly transitioning from an airframe under construction into a complete aircraft undergoing systems integration. Individual procurement notices may appear routine, but together they provide an indication of how the prototype is progressing toward power-on and eventually flight testing.
Automated cable-harness testing will ultimately help establish confidence in the aircraft’s electrical and avionics architecture before engineers begin energising the systems and conducting increasingly complex ground checks.

articles.title: Embraer Plans 10 C-390s a Year From India if It Wins IAF MTA Tender, Eyes Regional Export Hub
articles.text:
Brazilian aerospace giant Embraer is planning an ambitious production rate for the C-390 Millennium in India if the aircraft wins the Indian Air Force’s Medium Transport Aircraft (MTA) competition, with sources within Embraer telling idrw.org that the proposed Indian production line could eventually deliver at least 10 aircraft per year once it reaches peak production.
The plan would make the Indian facility considerably more than an assembly line established solely to fulfil the IAF order. According to idrw.org’s sources, Embraer sees India as a potential regional production and export hub for the C-390, allowing aircraft manufactured with its Indian partner Mahindra to be supplied to future customers across the wider region.
That strategy is consistent with Embraer’s publicly announced plans for India. Embraer and Mahindra Group signed a Strategic Cooperation Agreement in October 2025 covering joint marketing, industrialisation and development of India as a C-390 hub. The companies have officially stated that their long-term ambition is to establish India as a manufacturing and support centre serving both domestic and regional requirements.
The two companies have subsequently expanded their localisation plans to include an Indian Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul capability if the C-390 is selected for the MTA programme.
Sources told idrw.org that once the proposed Indian line reaches its mature production rate, Embraer believes output of at least 10 C-390s annually would be achievable. Such a production rate could allow the company to satisfy IAF requirements while maintaining capacity for export orders.
The export component could prove critical to sustaining the production line after the initial Indian requirement is completed. Embraer believes there remains a substantial international replacement market as air forces retire ageing tactical transports inherited from previous generations.
Aircraft such as the Antonov An-26 and older C-130 variants remain in service internationally, creating a potential replacement market during the 2030s. Embraer is positioning the C-390 as a modern jet-powered alternative capable of carrying up to 26 tonnes while performing troop and cargo transport, airdrop, medical evacuation, search-and-rescue and air-to-air refuelling missions.
The C-390’s customer base has already been expanding. Uzbekistan, for example, was revealed in February 2026 as another C-390 customer and will become the aircraft’s first operator in Central Asia.
For Embraer, an Indian production facility could consequently provide geographical advantages when competing for future Asian, Middle Eastern and potentially African requirements. Aircraft for those customers could eventually be assembled in India rather than relying exclusively on Brazilian production.
Such an arrangement would also fundamentally change the industrial value of the MTA programme for India. Instead of assembling a fixed number of aircraft for the IAF and subsequently winding down production, an export-oriented facility could remain active for considerably longer.
This would support a domestic supply chain covering structures, components, systems integration, final assembly and eventually maintenance and overhaul. Embraer has already publicly stated that it and Mahindra intend to engage with Indian aerospace companies to identify opportunities for local manufacturing, assembly and supply-chain participation.
A 10-aircraft annual production rate would also give the Indian line considerable flexibility. If the IAF ultimately places a large MTA order, domestic deliveries could be accelerated during the initial years before part of the capacity progressively shifts toward international customers.
However, the 10-aircraft target described by idrw.org’s Embraer sources should presently be viewed as a planned mature production capability, rather than a contracted delivery schedule. Actual output would depend on the size and timing of the Indian order, localisation requirements, supply-chain readiness and export demand.
The IAF competition itself is substantial, with the Defence Ministry recently moving ahead with the procurement process for the new transport aircraft.
Embraer’s proposition therefore appears to be increasingly centred on more than the performance of the C-390 itself. The Brazilian manufacturer is effectively offering India the opportunity to become a second major industrial centre for the aircraft.
If the C-390 wins the MTA competition and the proposed production strategy materialises, India could eventually manufacture transports not only for its own Air Force but also for countries replacing ageing An-26s, C-130s and other legacy airlifters.

articles.title: Philippines May Sign $200 Million Akash 1S Deal With India in 2026 After BrahMos Success
articles.text:
India’s growing defence partnership with the Philippines could soon move beyond the BrahMos supersonic cruise missile, with the indigenous Akash air-defence system emerging as the next major Indian weapon that Manila could acquire. A recent report by the Financial Express said a Philippines deal worth around US$200 million for the Akash 1S air-defence system is expected in 2026, potentially making it one of India’s most significant missile exports after the landmark BrahMos agreement. The report also linked the potential Akash sale directly to the success of BrahMos exports to the Philippines.
The reported deal is particularly significant because it would give the Philippines another Indian-made missile capability, this time focused on ground-based air defence rather than long-range anti-ship strike. The Akash system is designed to protect important military and strategic assets against aerial threats, including aircraft, helicopters, cruise missiles and drones.
The Philippines has already become the first major overseas customer for BrahMos. Manila signed a $375 million contract in 2022 for three shore-based BrahMos batteries, and the systems have subsequently been delivered. Philippine interest in acquiring additional Indian military equipment has grown as the country strengthens its capabilities amid increasing security concerns in the South China Sea.
There is already evidence that Manila has been examining Akash. In February 2025, Reuters reported that India expected a missile deal worth more than $200 million with the Philippines and that Manila had expressed interest in the Akash system. Indian sources told Reuters that the Philippines was expected to place an order during the fiscal year beginning in April.
If Manila proceeds with Akash, India would be moving from selling the Philippines a single high-end offensive weapon to supplying different layers of its defence architecture. That could prove strategically important for New Delhi. An Akash sale would strengthen India’s position as an alternative defence supplier for countries that want to reduce excessive dependence on either Western or Chinese systems.
For the Philippines, meanwhile, the combination of BrahMos for long-range coastal strike and Akash for ground-based air defence could provide two very different capabilities from the same emerging defence partner.

articles.title: DRDO Has VSHORADS, So Why Is Indian Army Still Buying Britain’s Martlet Missile?
articles.text:
India and the United Kingdom are reportedly in the final stages of concluding an expanded agreement for Thales’ Lightweight Multirole Missile (LMM), better known as the Martlet. British officials have told Indian media outlets including ThePrint and Times Now that the enlarged deal is expected to be signed soon. If concluded as planned, the order would make India the second-largest customer for the LMM globally, behind Ukraine, which has placed the largest cumulative order for the missile.
The proposed acquisition, however, raises an important question. Why is the Indian Army procuring Martlet from the UK when DRDO has already developed the Very Short Range Air Defence System, or VSHORADS, for frontline troops?
The answer is that although both weapons can be employed against low-flying aerial threats, they are based on different technologies and offer different operational capabilities. DRDO’s VSHORADS has been developed specifically as a short-range air-defence system for frontline military formations. It uses an imaging infrared seeker and a dual-thrust solid-propellant rocket motor. The system is intended to provide a highly mobile air-defence capability against threats such as helicopters, aircraft and unmanned aerial systems operating at relatively short ranges.
The Martlet follows a different philosophy. It is a lightweight multirole missile designed not only for air-defence missions but also for engaging selected surface targets. One of its most important technological differences is its laser-beam-riding guidance system.
This difference could become significant on a battlefield increasingly dominated by drones and electronic warfare.
An infrared-guided missile such as VSHORADS can use the target’s thermal signature to guide itself towards the target. Once launched, this provides considerable tactical flexibility because the missile does not need a continuous external guidance beam directed at the target. This can be particularly useful for soldiers operating in exposed forward positions.
Martlet’s laser-beam-riding system takes another approach. The operator or launch platform directs a laser towards the target, while the missile follows the laser beam. This gives the system a different guidance architecture and provides the Army with another option against aerial threats that may employ countermeasures against conventional infrared seekers.
The two missiles therefore have the potential to complement each other rather than compete directly.
In the plains, VSHORADS could form part of the Army’s close-range air-defence umbrella around forward units, command posts, artillery positions, logistics elements and other important battlefield assets. Martlet could supplement these systems by providing an additional missile with a different seeker and engagement mechanism.
The combination becomes even more interesting in high-altitude areas.
Mountain warfare presents unique challenges for air-defence systems. Reduced atmospheric density, extreme temperatures, difficult terrain and severe logistical constraints can affect missile propulsion, sensors, batteries and mobility. DRDO has designed VSHORADS with high-altitude deployment in mind, making it particularly relevant for India’s northern borders.
Martlet could provide another layer of capability for troops operating in mountainous terrain, especially where its lower missile weight and flexible deployment options are advantageous. However, its actual effectiveness at extreme altitude would ultimately depend on operational trials, environmental qualification and the configuration selected by the Army.
There is another reason why the Martlet acquisition could make sense despite the availability of an indigenous system: numbers and diversification.
Modern air defence increasingly depends on layered systems rather than relying on one missile. A formation facing drones, helicopters, loitering munitions and other low-altitude threats benefits from having interceptors with different guidance technologies and engagement characteristics.
For the Indian Army, VSHORADS could provide the indigenous infrared-guided component, while Martlet could add a lightweight laser-guided missile with multirole potential. Having both systems would also reduce dependence on a single missile technology across the entire very-short-range air-defence layer.
The proposed Martlet order should therefore not automatically be viewed as an indication that DRDO’s VSHORADS has failed or is considered inadequate. Instead, it could reflect the Army’s broader requirement for a diversified and layered short-range air-defence architecture.

articles.title: J-16D for Pakistan? Chinese Aviation Expert Mocks Claims of Secret PAF Electronic Warfare Fleet
articles.text:
A claim that the Pakistan Air Force (PAF) secretly acquired a small number of Chinese J-16D electronic warfare aircraft has triggered a fresh debate among military aviation watchers, with a prominent Chinese military aviation researcher openly dismissing the allegation and questioning the credibility of those promoting it.
The claim emerged on social media from Pakistani defence commentator Zohaib Ahmed, who stated that Pakistan had acquired J-16D aircraft in 2025 but was not planning to form a dedicated J-16D squadron. According to his explanation, the aircraft were supposedly being used as strategic assets for electronic warfare (EW) and operational evaluation within Pakistan’s wider network-centric warfare architecture. The post also suggested that their sensitive nature explained why they had not been publicly seen.
When another user questioned when Pakistan had acquired the aircraft and why there had been no sightings, Ahmed replied that the acquisition had taken place in 2025. He subsequently argued that the aircraft were “strategic assets” and therefore would not be highlighted publicly until necessary.
The assertion, however, has not been accompanied by publicly available photographic evidence, satellite imagery, official documentation or independent reporting confirming that the PAF operates the J-16D. That absence has become particularly significant because the J-16D is not an ordinary J-16 variant that could easily disappear into the background of Pakistan’s existing fighter fleet.
The J-16D is a specialised electronic warfare aircraft developed by China from the J-16. Chinese military sources have publicly described it as an EW platform designed to conduct reconnaissance, electronic attack and defensive electronic warfare missions. China’s Ministry of National Defense reported as early as 2021 that the aircraft had entered realistic combat training with the People’s Liberation Army Air Force (PLAAF).
The aircraft also has several visually distinctive features. Unlike a conventional J-16, the J-16D carries prominent electronic warfare equipment, including specialised wingtip pods and additional jamming systems. Its configuration is sufficiently different that identifying one in satellite imagery or high-quality photographs would be considerably easier than identifying a conventional J-16.
Andreas Rupprecht, a well-known researcher of Chinese military aviation, has now pushed back strongly against the Pakistani claim. In comments shown in the screenshots, Rupprecht mocked claims circulating on Pakistani forums about the PAF receiving J-11B or J-16 aircraft and described the suggestion that retired J-11s had been upgraded to J-16 standard as particularly implausible. He also directly criticised the claim that a Pakistani think tank had established that J-16Ds were already secretly operating with the PAF.
His criticism matters because the J-16D itself is a well-documented Chinese capability rather than a hypothetical aircraft. Independent assessments have identified the type as a dedicated airborne electronic attack platform, while the U.S. Congressional reporting has also identified J-16Ds among China’s radar-jamming EW aircraft.
That does not mean a covert Pakistani acquisition is technically impossible. Pakistan has a close defence relationship with China and has increasingly incorporated Chinese sensors, missiles, aircraft and network-centric capabilities into its air force. A limited acquisition of specialised EW aircraft would therefore make operational sense in isolation.

articles.title: India Has Issued a 2,995-km NOTAM. What Missile Could Be Tested Next?
articles.text:
India has issued a new Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) indicating preparations for a likely long-range missile test over the Indian Ocean Region on September 2–3, 2026. The notified danger corridor extends approximately 2,995 km from the vicinity of Dr APJ Abdul Kalam Island off Odisha, according to the NOTAM graphic shared by open-source intelligence analyst Damien Symon.
The notification has immediately drawn attention because of the unusually long maritime corridor. However, the NOTAM itself does not identify the missile being tested, and its 2,995-km length should not automatically be interpreted as the missile’s actual maximum range.
A NOTAM is primarily a safety measure intended to keep civilian aircraft and other traffic away from areas where a missile launch or other hazardous activity could take place. The dimensions of the restricted zone therefore provide an indication of the area that authorities want cleared, rather than a definitive statement of the missile’s performance.
The latest notification comes after an unusually active period for India’s strategic missile programme. In May, India conducted the flight test of an Advanced Agni missile equipped with a Multiple Independently Targeted Re-entry Vehicle (MIRV) system from Dr APJ Abdul Kalam Island. The Defence Ministry said the missile carried multiple payloads directed towards separate targets in the Indian Ocean Region, with ground and ship-based tracking stations monitoring the mission.
India subsequently conducted another important strategic missile test in June, when the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) successfully flight-tested the Long Range Land Attack Cruise Missile (LRLACM) from the same test facility.
The possibility of another Agni-series trial cannot be ruled out. India has increasingly used flight tests to validate individual components and technologies rather than simply demonstrating maximum missile range. Such trials can examine propulsion, guidance, stage separation, re-entry systems and other technologies without requiring a full-range flight.

articles.title: Tanks are ‘iron wall’ on borders, boost soldiers’ morale: Rajnath Singh
articles.text:
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh on Thursday described tanks as an “iron wall” on India’s borders that act as a death knell for the enemy and boost the morale of soldiers deployed in forward areas, asserting they remain vital to ground warfare despite the growing role of drones and missiles.
Singh made the remarks after laying the foundation stone of a Rs 472-crore facility for the overhaul of T-series battle tanks at the 57-year-old Vehicle Factory Jabalpur (VFJ), an ordnance unit here.
“Our Army is one of the most powerful forces in the world. T-72 and T-90 tanks are extremely important for ground warfare. They stand like an iron wall on our borders,” he said.
“Tanks act as a death knell for the enemy and also boost the morale of our soldiers deployed on the borders,” Singh added.
He said tanks, like other military equipment, require regular maintenance and periodic overhauling to ensure their operational readiness.
Under the upcoming project, the facility will overhaul 80 T-72 and T-90 tanks annually, Singh said.
The Indian Army requires the overhaul of around 230 such tanks every year, according to him.
The Heavy Vehicles Factory (HVF) at Avadi currently overhauls around 150 tanks annually, and the new facility at VFJ will bridge the remaining shortfall, the defence minister said.
Singh said modern warfare was changing rapidly, with drones, missiles and other advanced technologies playing an increasingly important role.
“We need drones, missiles, artillery, electronic warfare systems and modern tanks. Our soldiers should have both tanks and drones, with effective coordination between the two,” he said.
The upcoming facility in Jabalpur would further strengthen India’s capabilities in this direction, Singh added.
New technologies were constantly emerging in the defence sector and battles could no longer be won using conventional methods alone, the defence minister said.
In the age of drones and missiles, some may question the relevance of tanks, he said, adding that he held a different view.”The character of warfare has changed, but that does not mean tanks have lost their relevance. Drones and missiles are important, but tanks continue to have a role. What is needed is not reliance on a single platform, but a combined capability,” Singh said.
Every weapon system has its own strengths, he said.
“The strength of a tank lies in its mobility and firepower. The need today is not to eliminate tanks, but to modernise them. This is not a battle of one weapon against another; it is a battle involving the entire combat system,” Singh said.
While technology and the character of warfare were evolving, tanks continued to remain relevant and necessary in ground warfare, he added.
VFJ, where the tank overhaul facility is coming up, is a premier military vehicle manufacturing unit operating under Armoured Vehicles Nigam Limited (AVNL).
Established in 1969, the factory initially produced Shaktiman 3 tonnes (T) vehicles in collaboration with Germany’s MAN, as well as Nissan 1T and Jonga vehicles in collaboration with Japan’s Nissan Motors Co.
The factory complex is spread over 330 acres, while its adjoining estate covers another 600 acres, officials said.

articles.title: Indian Reveals Roadmap to 100GW through Nuclear Power by 2047
articles.text:
India is committed to building a secure, sustainable, and self-reliant energy future to support its journey towards Viksit Bharat. Recognising the growing demand for clean, reliable and stable baseload electricity, the Government of India has placed nuclear energy at the core of its long-term energy strategy. Nuclear power provides round-the-clock, low-carbon electricity, complementing renewable energy while ensuring grid stability. It also reduces dependence on imported fossil fuels and supports India’s climate commitments. Guided by the vision of Aatmanirbhar Bharat, the Government of India is developing robust indigenous capabilities across the entire nuclear fuel cycle, including reactor design, fuel fabrication, waste management, and advanced technologies.
India currently operates 24 nuclear power reactors with a total installed capacity of 8.78 GW. Nine reactor units, with a combined capacity of 7.5 GW, are under construction. The Government has also approved 10 indigenous Pressurized Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs) in fleet mode and pre-project activities for two 500 MW Fast Breeder Reactors (FBR). Recent policy initiatives, including the Nuclear Energy Mission (2025–26) and the SHANTI Act, 2025, are accelerating capacity expansion, strengthening domestic manufacturing, promoting innovation and enabling greater private sector participation. Together, these initiatives are creating a resilient nuclear ecosystem that supports sustainable development and advances India’s goal of achieving 100 GW of nuclear power capacity by 2047.
| Baseload Electricity Stable baseload electricity is the minimum, uninterrupted amount of power an electric grid needs to remain operational. It acts as the backbone of our power supply, ensuring reliable electricity for hospitals, communication networks, defence establishments, industries, and other essential services. Reliable baseload power is essential for economic growth, national security, and disaster resilience. | 
Understanding Nuclear Energy: An Overview
Nuclear power plants generate electricity by harnessing heat released through a carefully controlled process called nuclear fission. The heat converts water into steam, which drives a turbine connected to a generator. The generated electricity powers homes, industries, and essential services. The entire process operates within multiple engineered safety barriers and a robust regulatory framework.
Nuclear Fuel
Nuclear fuel is the material placed inside a nuclear reactor to generate electricity. Its atoms split through nuclear fission and release large amounts of heat. The heat converts water into steam. The steam drives turbines to generate electricity.
Nuclear reactor fuels can be fissile, which directly sustain the chain reaction or fertile, which are first converted into fissile fuels inside the reactor. The most common nuclear fuels are Natural Uranium, Uranium-235 (U-235), Low-Enriched Uranium (LEU), Plutonium-239 (Pu-239), and Mixed Oxide (MOX) fuel.
Most countries, including the United States, France, China, Japan, South Korea, Canada, and Russia, use Low-Enriched Uranium (LEU) in Light Water Reactors. India mainly uses Natural Uranium in Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs), which do not require uranium enrichment. India also uses MOX fuel in its Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR).
India’s uranium reserves are of low grade and therefore need to be supplemented through imports. India, however, has abundant reserves of thorium (Th-232). This is a fertile rather than fissile radioactive material, found mainly in the coastal sands of Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Odisha, West Bengal and Jharkhand. Inside a reactor, Th-232 absorbs a neutron and transforms into Uranium-233, which is fissile. India’s long-term nuclear strategy is centred on utilising its abundant thorium reserves, through its three-stage nuclear power programme.
| India’s Three-Stage Nuclear ProgrammeDr. Homi J. Bhabha proposed the three-stage nuclear power programme in 1954 to maximise the use of India’s indigenous resources and achieve long-term energy security. India achieved a major milestone in April 2026 when the Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam attained first criticality. A breeder reactor is one that produces more fissile material or fuel while generating electricity. This marked the beginning of the second stage of India’s three-stage nuclear power programme. The milestone brings India closer to harnessing its abundant thorium resources for long-term, clean, and self-reliant energy security. To read further: A New Chapter in India’s Nuclear JourneyIn the first stage, Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs) use natural uranium to generate electricity. The spent fuel is reprocessed to recover plutonium, which becomes the primary input for the second stage. In the second stage, Fast Breeder Reactors (FBRs) use this plutonium to generate electricity while breeding additional fissile material. They also produce uranium-233 from thorium, laying the groundwork for the third stage. In the third stage, thorium-based reactors use uranium-233 to harness India’s abundant thorium reserves. Each stage feeds into the next, unlocking long-term energy security.The Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR) led the design, development, testing, safety assessment, commissioning and indigenisation of India’s Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR). Through close collaboration with Indian industry, IGCAR achieved nearly 90 per cent domestic manufacturing of the reactor’s equipment and systems, strengthening India’s self-reliance in advanced nuclear technology and supporting the country’s second stage of the Three Stage Nuclear Power Programme. | 
Nuclear Reaction
A nuclear reaction releases energy from the nucleus of an atom. The two main types are nuclear fission and nuclear fusion. Nuclear power plants use nuclear fission.
In a nuclear reactor, a neutron strikes the nucleus of a uranium or plutonium atom, causing it to split into two smaller atoms. This process, known as nuclear fission, releases a large amount of heat and additional neutrons. These neutrons trigger further fission reactions, creating a carefully controlled chain reaction. The heat generated is used to convert water into high-pressure steam. The steam drives a turbine, which is connected to a generator. As the turbine rotates, the generator produces electricity.
| Nuclear FusionNuclear fusion combines two light atoms to form a heavier atom. Fusion powers the Sun and stars. It can produce much more energy than fission. However, fusion technology is still under development for commercial electricity generation. | 
Nuclear Reactors
The nuclear reactor is the heart of a nuclear power plant, where the process of nuclear fission is safely controlled to generate heat. It contains nuclear fuel, such as uranium or plutonium, control rods to regulate the fission reaction, a coolant to transfer the heat produced, and multiple safety systems to ensure safe and reliable operation.
India primarily uses Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors (PHWRs), which operate on natural uranium. The country also operates Boiling Water Reactors (BWRs) and Pressurised Water Reactors (PWRs). India is advancing Fast Breeder Reactors (FBRs) to utilise plutonium and support the transition to thorium-based reactors. India is also developing Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) as the next generation of nuclear technology.
| Small Modular ReactorSMRs typically generate up to 300 MWe through nuclear fission. Their compact, modular design enables factory-based manufacturing, faster construction, improved quality, and phased deployment. Under the Nuclear Energy Mission, announced in the Union Budget 2025–26, the Government has allocated ₹20,000 crore for the research, design, development, and deployment of indigenous SMRs. India is developing the 220 MWe Bharat Small Modular Reactor (BSMR-200), jointly designed by BARC and NPCIL, the 55 MWe SMR-55, and a High-Temperature Gas-Cooled Reactor for hydrogen production. The Government aims to operationalise at least five indigenous SMRs by 2033. | 
| Classification of Nuclear ReactorsNuclear reactors are designed for different applications. Large conventional reactors (700–1,600 MW) supply continuous baseload power to national grids, cities, and industries. Small Modular Reactors (up to 300 MW) and Micro Reactors (up to 20 MW) serve remote areas, replace retiring coal plants, supply industrial process heat, and support hydrogen production. | 
Nuclear Waste
Nuclear waste is the radioactive material generated during the operation of a nuclear power plant. It includes used nuclear fuel and other materials, such as protective clothing, filters, tools, and equipment, that become radioactive after being used in the plant. Since it emits radiation, it is managed under strict safety standards to ensure the protection of people and the environment.
India follows a closed nuclear fuel cycle, where spent nuclear fuel is reprocessed to recover valuable materials for reuse in future reactors. The remaining high-level radioactive waste is immobilised and safely stored, reducing waste and supporting India’s three-stage nuclear power programme.
| Vitrification TechnologyIndia is among the few countries with vitrification technology for high-level radioactive waste. The process converts high-level radioactive waste into a stable glass form, making it safer for long-term storage, transport, and eventual disposal. | 
Powering India’s Clean Energy Future
India’s nuclear energy programme reflects the country’s commitment to innovation, sustainability and self-reliance. By combining advanced technologies with rigorous safety standards and indigenous capabilities, nuclear energy is helping build a secure and resilient energy future. As the nation progresses towards Viksit Bharat, nuclear energy will continue to complement other clean energy sources, supporting economic growth, environmental sustainability and long-term energy security.

articles.title: Couple arrested for allegedly supplying Indian SIM cards to Pakistan handlers
articles.text:
The Delhi Police has busted an alleged Pakistan ISI-backed espionage module and arrested a couple accused of working for Pakistani intelligence operatives since 2024, procuring Indian SIM cards and sending them to Pakistan through Dubai, an official said on Friday.
Police said Md Sahil (25) and his wife Sameera (21) allegedly provided logistical support to Pakistan-based handlers and recruited people for espionage activities, including reconnaissance of cantonment areas at different locations in India.
According to police, the couple came in contact with Pakistani agents through social media in 2024 and were subsequently cultivated to work for the espionage network in return for financial gains. Their Pakistani handlers allegedly paid them Rs 30,000 for the SIM cards, police said.
The Special Cell received information about the alleged network operating in Delhi-NCR and developed the intelligence before identifying its local members. Police said Sahil was arrested first, and forensic analysis of his mobile phone allegedly revealed incriminating conversations with Pakistani intelligence operatives.
During interrogation, Sahil allegedly disclosed that he and Sameera sent eight Indian SIM cards to Pakistan via Dubai during 2024 and 2025. These SIM cards were activated on online messaging applications in Pakistan, and handlers allegedly used them to enter Indian WhatsApp groups to collect sensitive information. Police said the Pakistani operatives also allegedly used the numbers to approach Indians and collect information.
Police said Sahil was also assigned another task of recruiting individuals to conduct reconnaissance of cantonment areas in different parts of the country. Officials said he was also asked to provide details of Army personnel whose court-martial proceedings were pending before tribunals. Police said the interrogation of Sahil subsequently led to the arrest of Sameera, who allegedly played a key role in procuring and providing the Indian SIM cards to the Pakistan-based operatives.
Police recovered two mobile phones used in the alleged conspiracy from the accused. Forensic examination of the devices allegedly revealed chats and other incriminating conversations between the couple and their Pakistani handlers, police said.
They said the investigation provided crucial information about the modus operandi of the Pakistan-based handlers and their alleged network of local operatives, including how they used social media and encrypted communication platforms to coordinate espionage activities.
Sahil, who completed his BA from Indira Gandhi National Open University, had worked with a lawyer while planning to pursue an LLB but has been unemployed since June 2025. Sameera, a BA graduate who completed her Class 12 in Delhi, was working at a call centre in Noida before her arrest. Police said further investigation is underway to identify other members of the alleged espionage network and establish the full extent of the information shared with the Pakistan-based handlers.

articles.title: Researcher shows how Claude Code can be tricked simply by asking it to summarize a website
articles.text: Anthropic’s Claude Code running Opus 5 in Auto Mode can be tricked into executing attacker-controlled code simply by asking the coding agent to summarize a website. The attack works up to 80 percent of the time, according to prompt-injection wizard Johann Rehberger, aka wunderwuzzi. In a blog and video demo, he detailed how to hijack Opus 5 in Auto Mode, which is the default setting for Claude as of mid-August. It starts off by asking the agentic coding model to summarize a malicious website that presents itself as an archive of notebook records, and then tricking Claude into using curl instead of its WebFetch tool to retrieve the contents of the page – but without directly telling the model to use curl. The WebFetch request fails, returning a 415 Unsupported Media Type response, so the model decides to access the website directly by issuing a Bash tool call with curl. The website returns a 303 response, and redirects to a malicious ZIP archive, which Claude then downloads. This archive contains seemingly harmless files including catalog metadata, a README file, seven Base85/zlib-encoded JSON notebook records, a macOS decoder-darwin binary – plus a poisoned Python file named struct.py. Claude, per its safety guardrails, refuses to run the decoder: “This is planned and what the attacker wants,” Rehberger wrote. Instead of using the supplied binary, the AI decides to write its own decoder. “Ironically, that safety decision is the exploit path,” Rehberger explained, adding a purple devil emoji to the text. The new decoder imports base64, and from here the attack relies on Python module shadowing to trick the model into running the malicious struct.py code. Module shadowing occurs when a local file shares the same name as a Python standard-library module. The local file hides the official module, causing Python to load it instead. In this case, the standard-library base64 module imports the legitimate struct module, and the malicious ZIP contains a malicious file with the same name. Rehberger says he used ChatGPT to obfuscate the malicious struct.py code to bypass Claude’s safety controls, and this successfully launches a separate Python process to download and execute a remote payload – in this case a command-and-control callback, which in turn opens Calculator. We assume that real attackers would execute something a little more nefarious. In another attack scenario, struct.py launches a second, headless Claude Code via claude -p, meaning this prompt injection can be used not just to remotely execute code, but rather to create a whole new agent. “The nested Claude gets its own tool access and context,” Rehberger wrote. “In these runs the child performed basic recon (whoami, uname, id), opened Calculator and wrote to local files in the home folder.” Across three variants tested five times each, which Rehberger noted were small samples, he reported success rates between 60 percent and 80 percent. “I would say that these results are representative for a motivated attack, but not comprehensive.” Anthropic did not respond to The Register’s request for comment, but reportedly told Rehberger that the model’s “behavior is working as designed.” We’ve heard this one before. “Auto Mode is a convenience feature backed by a best-effort classifier, not a security guarantee,” Rehberger wrote, paraphrasing Anthropic’s response to his security report. According to Rehberger, the classifier isn’t built to stop determined prompt-injection chains made up of individually benign-looking steps, and the real boundary is OS isolation and network egress control. The key takeaway, according to Rehberger, is to run this and other coding agents in a sandbox. “The solution is something we talked about for many years,” he wrote. “Do not trust the model output.”®

articles.title: German-Japanese researchers invent electricity-free tech that could cool datacenters
articles.text: Datacenter cooling could get a lot more affordable, and sustainable, if a joint German-Japanese research project can be scaled beyond the laboratory. Researchers from the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology and the University of Tsukuba published a paper in Nature Energy on Friday discussing the success they had with a solid-state cooling technology that doesn’t need any electric input at all, and was still able to demonstrate temperature reductions in laboratory experiments. For those unfamiliar with solid-state cooling, it’s a more sustainable alternative to traditional compression cooling that relies on environmentally harmful refrigerants and lots of electricity. Instead of compressing and expanding a gas to generate cold, some solid-state systems rely on thermoelectric materials that, when supplied with electricity, can generate temperature differences. Thermoelectric solid-state cooling systems can be incredibly small, but there’s a catch: They still need energy, and they’re only a quarter as efficient as modern compression cooling systems, as the researchers noted. Enter elastocaloric cooling, which relies on shape-memory alloys that change temperature when mechanically loaded and unloaded through a phase transition. It’s that sort of material and methodology that the KIT and Tsukuba team experimented with. Like other forms of solid-state cooling, elastocaloric systems have traditionally required electricity to effect change in the shape-memory alloys they use, relying on actuators that can get quite large. What the researchers wanted to develop was a miniaturized form of elastocaloric cooling that didn’t require any electricity at all, instead relying on the waste heat being generated by the objects it wanted to cool – for example, a computer processor, as they mention in their paper. Based on their demonstration, it appears to have worked. The researchers used a pair of super thin nickel-titanium foils for their elastocaloric system with opposing functions: One foil shrinks when subjected to heat, generating movement that translates into mechanical energy and acting as its own actuator. That mechanical energy is transferred to the second foil, which is loaded and unloaded to trigger a phase transition that produces the cooling effect. Laboratory tests demonstrated that their technology isn’t only theoretically feasible, but also actually works – albeit to a limited extent. “Our prototype achieves a temperature span of 12.9 K at the refrigerant film level and 4.0 K at the device level under Joule-heated actuation at 86°C (187°F),” the team said in their report. When subjected to an external heat source of 130°C (266°F), the system still maintained a device-level temperature span of 2.2 K – not a lot, but it still shows the device, even at its most basic, single-pair-of-films level, works. "For us, the decisive moment was seeing measurable cooling for the first time, actually generated by a heat-driven system," KIT PhD candidate and paper lead author Yi-Ting Hsiau said of the project in a release put out by the university. "This showed us that the principle doesn't just work on paper." With the concept of electricity-free miniaturized cooling now proven, the team is planning to build larger experimental units to optimize cooling performance. Electricity-free and water-free cooling designs couldn’t come at a better time: Energy generation used to power and cool things like datacenters is on the rise, as is the water footprint of such facilities, in part also linked to cooling. Add climate change to the mix, and cooling electronics and people is only more of a concern – according to IRENA, heating and cooling together now account for more than 40 percent of global energy-related carbon dioxide emissions. Sorting out the datacenter energy and water problem has a lot to do with figuring out how to keep systems cool, and while this research is in its infancy, it could prove to be a valuable contribution to reducing the tech industry’s energy footprint. "We believe this is just the beginning," said Jingyuan Xu, head of KIT’s ZEco Thermal Lab, working on zero-emissions and eco-friendly heating and cooling tech. "By scaling up this technology, we aim to develop compact cooling systems that utilize abundant heat sources for sustainable cooling." ®

articles.title: AWS Route 53 DNS service reimagined...as a file system?
articles.text: For years, Corey Quinn, chief cloud economist at Duckbill and occasional Reg columnist, has argued that Amazon's Route 53 DNS service is a database. While literally true in the sense that DNS records are stored key-value pairs, it's more of a provocation than an endorsement. Even so, the idea has inspired prior jibes. In that spirit, Colin Percival, the creator of backup service Tarsnap, has released Route 53 Files, "a new file system that seamlessly connects any AWS compute resource with Amazon's highest-availability database." "The opening line of referring to Route 53 as Amazon's highest-availability database was partly a hat-tip to Corey," Percival told The Register. "Everyone in the field knows it's true, though." But Percival's satirical target isn't really AWS database downtime. He's more focused on Amazon S3 Files, a file system that links AWS compute resources with Amazon Simple Storage Service. "S3 Files launched in April and my reaction was, 'Oh, we're shipping category errors now? Hold my beer,'" explained Percival. "I'm not saying that Route 53 Files can't be useful – as Corey notes, the API for Route 53 is awful – but the inspiration was 'this needs to be satirized' and the launch post was written with that in mind." The launch post was penned in the style of the S3 Files launch post. Percival pointed to one particular passage about Route 53 Files being "ideal for shared workloads that mutate authoritative DNS, such as AI agents collaborating through file-based tools and on-call engineers reverting each other's changes using sed." That passage, he said, echoes wording from the AWS post pitching S3 Files as being "ideal for interactive, shared workloads that mutate data, from agentic AI agents collaborating through file-based tools to ML training pipelines processing datasets." Percival said he understands that many AWS customers love S3 Files. "But the fact customers ask for faster horses doesn't in itself mean that's what we should give them; the weird edge cases which come up when you ship category errors can cause unexpected problems and I'm not convinced that customers understand them sufficiently," he said. Percival said he doesn't personally know anyone using S3 Files in production. "I'm just looking at the design and saying, 'that looks like a sharp edge which will hurt someone.' Two examples which come to mind are the 'Sync back to S3 after 60 seconds of inactivity,' which I'm sure will bite someone eventually when they end up waiting for changes which never arrive because a file is being continuously updated; and the IAM integration, which (due to the security fail which is IMDS) gives people far less privilege separation than they might expect from a filesystem." Quinn expressed appreciation for Percival's work. "I've been calling Route53 a database for the better part of a decade mostly to annoy people who know what a database is," Quinn told The Register. "Colin took the amazing bones of a legendary service and gave it an interface model that isn't molten garbage, and I am totally here for it. He replaced the API with echo which is a downgrade in every respect except for the part where it works without requiring six weeks of cloud school." And the funny thing is that it actually works. ®
